issues.legal_issue: A tenant settled on mortgaged land by a mortgagee in possession does not acquire occupancy rights binding on the mortgagor where the settlement is not bona fide or the mortgage terms prohibit the mortgagee from settling tenants.
material_facts: The land was the owners’ khudkasht land and was placed in the mortgagee’s possession under a zuripeshgi arrangement.
The mortgage deed required the mortgagee to cultivate the land himself, pay reserved rent, and take the produce on account of his mortgage interest.
The mortgagee settled the land with a tenant for a three-year term.
The tenant’s kabuliyat referred to the mortgagee’s interest and required the tenant to surrender possession at the end of the term without claiming that the land was his old kasht land.
The tenant and his successors remained in possession for over thirty years after the lease expired, until the mortgage was redeemed.
issues.conclusion: The settlement was not bona fide and was contrary to the mortgage terms, so the tenant and his successors acquired no permanent occupancy rights that could prevent the owners from recovering possession after redemption.
issues.legal_principle: A mortgagee cannot confer an interest extending beyond the mortgage or act to the mortgagor’s detriment; under section 76(a) and (e) of the Transfer of Property Act, a mortgagee in possession must manage the property prudently and must not commit acts destructive of or permanently injurious to it. A bona fide settlement made in prudent management may be an exception where statutory tenancy rights arise, but the exception does not apply if the mortgage terms expressly or by necessary implication prohibit settlements. The court relied on Bengal Indigo Company v. Roghobur Das concerning the security character of a zuripeshgi lease, and distinguished Manjhil-Lal Biswanath Shah Deo v. Shaikh Mohiuddin and Babu Bhairo Nath Ray v. Shanke Pahan; it also explained why Binda Lal Pakrashi v. Kalu Pramanik did not assist a tenant who knew of the lessor’s limited authority.

predicates.mortgage_possession_dispute: The proceeding concerns an owner seeking possession after a mortgage has ended and a tenant claims rights through a settlement made by the mortgagee in possession.
predicates.settlement_by_mortgagee: The mortgagee in possession placed the land with a tenant under a settlement.
predicates.mortgage_terms_prohibit_settlements: The mortgage arrangement required the mortgagee to use the land personally or otherwise showed that the mortgagee could not settle tenants on it.
predicates.tenant_knew_lessor_lacked_settlement_aut: The tenant’s agreement or the circumstances showed that the tenant knew the lessor held the land only through the mortgage and accepted an obligation to surrender it without claiming an independent pre-existing right.
predicates.tenant_acquires_no_occupancy_rights_bind: The tenant does not acquire occupancy rights that prevent the owner from recovering possession after the mortgage ends.

issues.definition: When an owner seeks possession after a mortgage and the mortgagee settled a tenant despite limits on that authority known to the tenant, the tenant does not acquire occupancy rights binding on the owner.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant taking land from a mortgagee who is neither a proprietor nor a tenure-holder does not become a settled raiyat entitled to occupancy rights under the statutory rules for settled raiyats merely by remaining in possession for the requisite period.
material_facts: The tenant and his predecessors occupied the land continuously from the settlement until the owners sought possession after redemption, a period exceeding thirty years.
The mortgagee was a mortgagee, not a proprietor, tenure-holder, or under-tenure-holder.
The evidence showed that the land had been delivered to the mortgagee so that he could cultivate it himself.
The tenants claimed occupancy rights under sections 20 and 21 of the Bihar Tenancy Act.
issues.conclusion: The tenants were not settled raiyats within the meaning of section 5 and therefore did not acquire occupancy rights under sections 20 and 21 of the Bihar Tenancy Act.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 20 and 21 of the Bihar Tenancy Act apply to settled raiyats. Under section 5(2), a raiyat is primarily a person who has acquired land to cultivate it himself or through family members; section 5(3) requires the raiyat to hold immediately under a proprietor or tenure-holder. A mortgagee who is neither a proprietor nor a tenure-holder cannot satisfy that required relationship, and prolonged possession alone does not make the tenant a settled raiyat.

predicates.tenant_claims_occupancy_by_long_possessi: The tenant relies on continuous occupation for the required period as the basis for occupancy rights.
predicates.landlord_is_mortgagee: The tenant took the land from a person holding it as mortgagee.
predicates.landlord_is_not_proprietor_or_tenure_hol: The person from whom the tenant took the land did not own the estate as proprietor and did not hold it as a tenure-holder or under-tenure-holder.
predicates.tenant_is_not_settled_raiyat_entitled_to: The tenant does not qualify as a settled raiyat entitled to statutory occupancy rights.

issues.definition: A tenant who relies on long possession but holds through a mortgagee who is not a proprietor or tenure-holder does not qualify as a settled raiyat entitled to occupancy rights.

issues.legal_issue: A party may not raise on appeal a new contention based on treating one part of a combined mortgage arrangement differently when that contention was not advanced below and the transactions were treated there as one arrangement.
material_facts: One share of the land had been given to the mortgagee under an oral transaction, and the appellants argued that no prohibition on settling tenants had been proved for that share.
The argument had not been raised in the courts below.
In those courts, the two mortgage arrangements had been treated as parts of one transaction with common rights and liabilities.
issues.conclusion: The court declined to allow the new contention to be raised for the first time on appeal.
issues.legal_principle: The court would not entertain an appellate contention that had not been taken in the courts below where the transactions had been treated there as a single arrangement for determining the parties’ rights and liabilities.

predicates.civil_appeal: The proceeding is a civil appeal.
predicates.distinct_transaction_argument_not_raised: A party relies on a distinction between transactions or parts of the property that was not argued in the courts below.
predicates.transactions_treated_as_one_below: The courts below treated the transactions as one arrangement with common rights and liabilities.

issues.definition: In a civil appeal, a new distinction between transactions is not considered when it was not raised below and the transactions were treated there as one arrangement.
